label: achiever (Bartle)
source_text: Achievers regard points-gathering and rising in levels as their main goal, and all is ultimately subserviant to this. Exploration is necessary only to find new sources of treasure, or improved ways of wringing points from it. Socialising is a relaxing method of discovering what other players know about the business of accumulating points, that their knowledge can be applied to the task of gaining riches. Killing is only necessary to eliminate rivals or people who get in the way, or to gain vast amounts of points (if points are awarded for killing other players). [...] Achievers are proud of their formal status in the game's built-in level hierarchy, and of how short a time they took to reach it.
description_draft: This means playing to master the game: gathering points, levels and treasure is the goal, formal rank the pride, and exploring, chatting or fighting matter only as means of raising the score.
nearest_existing: ambitious / performance_oriented / status_seeking: the plain traits are life-wide (rising in status, judging each task by its score); the typed version lives inside a game, with the game's own points, levels and treasure as the score and the other three ways of playing reduced to means.
notes: Bartle 1996, 'Hearts, clubs, diamonds, spades: players who suit MUDs', Journal of MUD Research 1(1); the author's own page, fetched raw and quoted from it. Axes in Bartle's words: "The x-axis goes from an emphasis on players (left) to an emphasis on the environment (right); the y-axis goes from acting with (bottom) to acting on (top)." Bartle's quadrant glosses: "Achievers are interested in doing things to the game, ie. in ACTING on the WORLD." and "Explorers are interested in having the game surprise them, ie. in INTERACTING with the WORLD." Bartle's 'subserviant' is his spelling. 'Master the game' is Bartle's own phrase ('The point of playing is to master the game, and make it do what you want it to do'). Strength: neutral in the source, neutral in the draft.
set_review: Four quadrants of Bartle's interest graph, acting on vs interacting with (y) by world vs players (x). Each draft opens 'This means playing to/for <object>' so the quadrant is readable off the set: master the game (acting on the world), find out how the game works (interacting with the world), the people (interacting with players), impose oneself on other players (acting on players). Then two or three concrete behaviours from Bartle's paragraph, then a closing clause that subordinates the other three activities, as each of Bartle's four paragraphs does. All four at 32 words. Strength mirrored: the killer draft keeps Bartle's joy at the victim's distress (the one member that is a vice, beside bullying / cruel); the other three are neutral. Bartle's 'Socialisers' is British spelling; label and draft are US. Bartle's axis sentence: "The x-axis goes from an emphasis on players (left) to an emphasis on the environment (right); the y-axis goes from acting with (bottom) to acting on (top)."

label: authoritarian (Baumrind)
source_text: The authoritarian parent attempts to shape, control, and evaluate the behavior and attitudes of the child in accordance with a set standard of conduct, usually an absolute standard, theologically motivated and formulated by a higher authority. She [parent] values obedience as a virtue and favors punitive, forceful measures to curb self-will at points where the child's actions or beliefs conflict with what she thinks is right conduct. She believes in keeping the child in his place, , in restricting his autonomy, and in assigning household responsibilities in order to inculcate respect for work. She regards the preservation of order and traditional structure as a highly valued end in itself. She does not encourage verbal give and take, believing that the child should accept her word for what is right
description_draft: This means holding one's children to an absolute standard of conduct: prizing obedience, punishing self-will forcefully, keeping them in their place with little autonomy, and brooking no discussion of what is right.
nearest_existing: authoritarian (plain; the queue's political sense: a state that watches, censors and polices) / strict / controlling / paternalistic: the typed version is the parent at home holding children to an absolute standard with obedience and punishment; plain strict demands results from people generally and has no punishment or 'my word is final'.
notes: Baumrind 1966, 'Effects of authoritative parental control on child behavior', Child Development 37(4), 887-907, p. 890, as quoted on a developmental-psychology teaching page (the devpsy.org page named in earlier plans now redirects there); the page's doubled comma ('in his place, , in restricting') is reproduced verbatim. Baumrind's prototype is gendered ('She [parent] ... his [child]'); the draft says 'one's children'. 'Theologically motivated and formulated by a higher authority' left out as period detail. Strength: Baumrind's paragraph is strong (punitive, forceful, curb self-will, keep the child in his place) and the draft matches it; this corner is the one Baumrind member near a corpus vice (strict, controlling).
set_review: Square on Maccoby & Martin's two dimensions, responsiveness (warmth) by demandingness (control). Each draft opens with the parent's basic stance toward the children so the corner is readable: holding to an absolute standard with no discussion (high control, low warmth), directing by reason and standing firm (high, high), accepting impulses and asking little (low control, high warmth), neither warm nor demanding (low, low). All four at 32 words, 'one's children' throughout. The three Baumrind corners are summarised from her own 1966 prototype paragraphs (pp. 889-891); the fourth from Darling's 1999 ERIC digest quoting Maccoby & Martin 1983, whose text is a two-line placement plus a hedge ('most parents of this type fall within the normal range'), so the neglectful draft comes out markedly milder than the corpus's plain neglectful and than Wikipedia's portrait (unaware, indifferent); flagged in its notes for Roger. Per the standards rule the poles are not forced anti-parallel: authoritarian and permissive each follow their own paragraph (obedience and punishment vs acceptance and self-regulation), and authoritative keeps Baumrind's both-and ('Both autonomous self-will and disciplined conformity are valued').

label: authoritative (Baumrind)
source_text: The authoritative parent attempts to direct the child's activities but in a rational, issue-oriented manner. She [parent] encourages verbal give and take, shares with the child the reasoning behind her policy, and solicits his objections when he refuses to conform. Both autonomous self-will and disciplined conformity are valued. Therefore she exerts firm control at points of parent-child divergence, but does not hem the child in with restrictions. She enforces her own perspective as an adult, but recognizes the child's individual interests and special ways. The authoritative parent affirms the child's present qualities, but also sets standards for future conduct. She uses reason, power, and shaping by regime and reinforcement to achieve her objectives, and does not base her decisions on group consensus or the individual child's desires.
description_draft: This means directing one's children by reason: explaining the thinking behind each rule, hearing out their objections, standing firm where they balk without hemming them in, and valuing self-will alongside disciplined conduct.
nearest_existing: nurturing / autonomy_respecting / strict: the typed version joins firm standards to reasoning and give-and-take with one's children; nurturing has the care without the firm standards, autonomy_respecting leaves the choice to the other person, strict has the bar without the explanation.
notes: Baumrind 1966, p. 891, as quoted on the same teaching page. 'Standing firm where they balk' renders 'exerts firm control at points of parent-child divergence' and 'solicits his objections when he refuses to conform'; 'without hemming them in' is Baumrind's phrase. Strength: Baumrind's text is the flattering corner by design (the style she championed) and the draft stays at that level, neither warmer nor firmer than the source.

label: boomer
source_text: [Pew] By this definition, both are shorter than the span of the Baby Boomers (19 years) – the only generation officially designated by the U.S. Census Bureau, based on the famous surge in post-WWII births in 1946 and a significant decline in birthrates after 1964. [...] [Wikipedia, Baby boomers] Theirs was a time of economic prosperity and rapid technological progress, and many grew up expecting the world to improve with time. However, young people felt a sense of alienation and sought to assert their own individuality, freedom, and authenticity. [...] [Wikipedia, OK boomer] The phrase has developed into a retort for resistance to technological change, climate change denial, marginalization of members of minority groups, or opposition to younger generations' values more generally.
description_draft: This means being born between 1946 and 1964: growing up in postwar prosperity expecting the world to keep improving, prizing individuality and freedom, and resisting new technology and younger generations' values.
nearest_existing: elderly / nostalgic / late_adopter / traditional: elderly is age alone (seventies or beyond); the typed version is a birth cohort (about 62 to 80 in 2026) with the stereotyped postwar optimism, sixties individualism, and resistance to new technology and to younger generations' values.
notes: Pew Research Center's 2019 definitions give the birth years and the formative events but no portrait; the conventional portrait is Wikipedia's, each sentence checked against the raw page. The queue's speech stereotypes (slang, typing habits) appear in none of the sources, so the draft carries habits and attitudes only; the label will have to carry the speech. Membership tag: the draft states the cohort plainly, no disclaimer. The 'Baby boomers' article is history (prosperity, optimism, the counterculture's individuality) and carries no present-day stereotype; that lives in the 'OK boomer' article, whose list of the attitudes the retort answers (resistance to technological change, climate change denial, marginalization of minority groups, opposition to younger generations' values) is the source of the draft's last clause. The draft takes the first and the general last item and leaves climate denial and marginalization out as the sharpest items; Roger may want one back. Strength: the source states these as the attitudes the meme mocks; the draft states them as the person's own habits, which is the inside-voice rendering, not a sharpening.
set_review: Sequence in birth order: each draft opens 'This means being born between <years>' with Pew's birth years (1946-1964, 1965-1980, 1981-1996, 1997-2012; Pew gives Gen Z's start only, the end year is Wikipedia's), so the order is readable off the set, then one formative-era clause and the cohort's stereotyped traits and habits from the Wikipedia portrait. All four at 32 words; the birth-year clause costs eight of them, which is why the portraits are tight. Pew supplies years and formative events (9/11, the recession, the computer revolution, the internet, the iPhone), Wikipedia the portraits. Speech stereotypes are in no source and are absent from all four drafts. The millennial 'entitled and narcissistic' stereotype is in the source as a contested claim (Twenge, with a critic quoted) and is left out of the draft; flagged for Roger in its notes. Strength: each portrait is at the Wikipedia level, which is plain for boomers (via OK boomer) and Gen X (slackers, cynical), mildly flattering for Gen Z (better behaved, less hedonistic).

label: conscientiousness (DISC)
source_text: The C (Conscientiousness) style is thoughtful and questioning. This describes people who are analytical, reserved, and precise. [...] Conversely, people with styles that fall toward the bottom of the circle tend to be more moderate-paced and are often described as calm, methodical, and careful. [...] People with DiSC styles that fall toward the left side of the circle are naturally more skeptical in nature and are often described as logic-focused, objective, and challenging.
description_draft: This means being moderate-paced and skeptical: analytical, reserved and precise, calm and methodical in how one works, focused on logic over people, and questioning and objective rather than going along.
nearest_existing: conscientious (plain: diligence, thoroughness, attention to detail) / analytical / precise / meticulous / skeptical: the typed version is analytical, precise and reserved with a questioning stance and a moderate pace; plain conscientious is dutifulness and reliability, which the typed version never mentions, so the shared word is misleading (Marston's original factor was compliance).
notes: Primary source is the publisher's (Wiley, Everything DiSC) own page, since the four labels are the publisher's names; the fuller style pages with priorities and motivators (discprofile.com/what-is-disc and its overview-styles PDF) returned HTTP 403 to every fetch, so they are not quoted. A search-engine snippet of that page (unverified, not used in the draft) listed the D style's priorities as getting immediate results, taking action, challenging self and others; i as expressing enthusiasm, taking action, encouraging collaboration; S as giving support, maintaining stability, enjoying collaboration; C as ensuring accuracy, maintaining stability, challenging assumptions. Marston 1928, Emotions of Normal People (public domain; full text at https://archive.org/stream/emotionsofnormal0000mars/emotionsofnormal0000mars_djvu.txt), names the four primary emotions dominance, inducement, submission and compliance on two axes, alliance vs antagonism of the stimulus and superiority vs inferiority of the self's strength; dominance is "chiefly characterized by victory of the motor self over an antagonist of inferior intensity", inducement introspectively "a process of persuading someone, in a friendly way, to perform an act suggested by the subject", submission the bodily attitude of "an obedient child toward a loving mother", compliance that "the subject is moving himself at the dictates of a superior force". Wikipedia's gloss (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DISC_assessment): "Dominance: active use of force to overcome resistance in the environment Inducement: use of charm in order to deal with obstacles Submission: warm and voluntary acceptance of the need to fulfill a request Compliance: fearful adjustment to a superior force." The modern S and C differ from Marston's submission and compliance, so his text is background, not the summarised source. Strength: the publisher's text is neutral and the draft matches it.
set_review: Square on the publisher's two dimensions, pace (active, fast-paced vs thoughtful, moderate-paced) by stance (questioning, skeptical vs accepting). Each draft opens 'This means being <pace> and <stance>' so the quadrant is readable off the set, then the style's three descriptors from the publisher's page, a pace clause and a stance clause. 30 to 32 words. The source is a publisher's blurb, uniformly neutral-to-flattering ('no one style is better or worse than the next'), so all four come out milder than their plain corpus neighbours (dominance beside dominant / controlling; conscientiousness beside conscientious / meticulous); mirrored, not sharpened. The stance clause is near-identical for the two members that share a side (i and S both 'people over logic'; D and C both 'logic over people'), which is the axis showing; they differ by pace. Marston 1928 is the system's origin, but his four primary emotions (dominance, inducement, submission, compliance) differ in content from the modern S and C, so he is recorded in notes, not summarised. The publisher's fuller page (discprofile.com) was 403 throughout; see notes.

label: dominance (DISC)
source_text: The D (Dominance) style is active and questioning. This describes people who are direct, forceful, and outspoken with their opinions. [...] People with DiSC styles at the top of the circle tend to be fast-paced and are often described as assertive, dynamic, and bold. [...] People with DiSC styles that fall toward the left side of the circle are naturally more skeptical in nature and are often described as logic-focused, objective, and challenging.
description_draft: This means being fast-paced and skeptical: direct, forceful and outspoken, bold and assertive in taking action, focused on logic over people, and challenging others rather than going along with them.
nearest_existing: dominant (plain: taking control of conversations, steering to outcomes, assertive leadership) / confident / blunt / competitive: the typed version adds pace and skepticism (fast, logic-focused, challenging) and is a neutral workplace style, milder than plain dominant's taking control of others; Marston's own dominance ('victory of the motor self over an antagonist') is closer to plain dominant.
notes: Primary source is the publisher's (Wiley, Everything DiSC) own page, since the four labels are the publisher's names; the fuller style pages with priorities and motivators (discprofile.com/what-is-disc and its overview-styles PDF) returned HTTP 403 to every fetch, so they are not quoted. A search-engine snippet of that page (unverified, not used in the draft) listed the D style's priorities as getting immediate results, taking action, challenging self and others; i as expressing enthusiasm, taking action, encouraging collaboration; S as giving support, maintaining stability, enjoying collaboration; C as ensuring accuracy, maintaining stability, challenging assumptions. Marston 1928, Emotions of Normal People (public domain; full text at https://archive.org/stream/emotionsofnormal0000mars/emotionsofnormal0000mars_djvu.txt), names the four primary emotions dominance, inducement, submission and compliance on two axes, alliance vs antagonism of the stimulus and superiority vs inferiority of the self's strength; dominance is "chiefly characterized by victory of the motor self over an antagonist of inferior intensity", inducement introspectively "a process of persuading someone, in a friendly way, to perform an act suggested by the subject", submission the bodily attitude of "an obedient child toward a loving mother", compliance that "the subject is moving himself at the dictates of a superior force". Wikipedia's gloss (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DISC_assessment): "Dominance: active use of force to overcome resistance in the environment Inducement: use of charm in order to deal with obstacles Submission: warm and voluntary acceptance of the need to fulfill a request Compliance: fearful adjustment to a superior force." The modern S and C differ from Marston's submission and compliance, so his text is background, not the summarised source. Strength: the publisher's D is 'direct, forceful, and outspoken', a style not a vice; the draft stays there and does not import Marston's force or the corpus's controlling.

label: explorer (Bartle)
source_text: Explorers delight in having the game expose its internal machinations to them. They try progressively esoteric actions in wild, out-of-the-way places, looking for interesting features (ie. bugs) and figuring out how things work. Scoring points may be necessary to enter some next phase of exploration, but it's tedious, and anyone with half a brain can do it. Killing is quicker, and might be a constructive exercise in its own right, but it causes too much hassle in the long run if the deceased return to seek retribution. Socialising can be informative as a source of new ideas to try out, but most of what people say is irrelevant or old hat. The real fun comes only from discovery, and making the most complete set of maps in existence.
description_draft: This means playing to find out how the game works: trying odd actions in far corners, hunting hidden features and bugs, mapping everything, and finding points, fights and chatter dull beside discovery.
nearest_existing: curious / inquisitive / exploratory: the plain traits are interest in topics and probing questions in conversation; the typed version is interest in a game's mechanics, bugs and map, and it actively disdains the scoreboard, which curious does not.
notes: Bartle 1996, 'Hearts, clubs, diamonds, spades: players who suit MUDs', Journal of MUD Research 1(1); the author's own page, fetched raw and quoted from it. Axes in Bartle's words: "The x-axis goes from an emphasis on players (left) to an emphasis on the environment (right); the y-axis goes from acting with (bottom) to acting on (top)." Bartle's quadrant glosses: "Achievers are interested in doing things to the game, ie. in ACTING on the WORLD." and "Explorers are interested in having the game surprise them, ie. in INTERACTING with the WORLD." 'Bugs' is Bartle's own gloss on 'interesting features'. Strength: neutral in the source (mild disdain for points and chatter), neutral in the draft.

label: gen-x
source_text: [Pew] Generation X (born between 1965 and 1980) [...] [Wikipedia] As children in the 1970s and 1980s, a time of shifting societal values, Gen Xers were sometimes called the "Latchkey Generation", a reference to their returning as children from school to an empty home Xers were dubbed the "MTV Generation" (a reference to the music video channel) and sometimes characterized as slackers, cynical, and disaffected. [...] In 2014, Pew Research provided further insight, describing the cohort as "savvy, skeptical and self-reliant; they're not into preening or pampering, and they just might not give much of a hoot what others think of them. [...] guides regarding managing multiple generations in the workforce describe Gen Xers as: independent, resilient, resourceful, self-managing, adaptable, cynical, pragmatic, skeptical of authority, and as seeking a work-life balance.
description_draft: This means being born between 1965 and 1980: coming home to an empty house after school, raised on music videos, and turning out independent, skeptical of authority and unconcerned what others think.
nearest_existing: independent / self_reliant / cynical / skeptical: the typed version is the cohort (about 46 to 61 in 2026) with the latchkey childhood and the slacker-skeptic image; plain cynical is distrust of human nature, which the typed version does not claim, and plain self_reliant sees a team as dead weight, which it does not.
notes: Pew Research Center's 2019 definitions give the birth years and the formative events but no portrait; the conventional portrait is Wikipedia's, each sentence checked against the raw page. The queue's speech stereotypes (slang, typing habits) appear in none of the sources, so the draft carries habits and attitudes only; the label will have to carry the speech. Membership tag: the draft states the cohort plainly, no disclaimer. Wikipedia's lead gives the same years as Pew ('generally defined as people born from 1965 to 1980'). The nicknames 'Latchkey Generation' and 'MTV Generation' are in the source and kept out of the draft, which renders them as the empty house and the music videos. 'Unconcerned what others think' renders Pew 2014's 'might not give much of a hoot what others think of them'. 'Slackers' is in the source and not in the draft (no room at 32; the draft's traits are the ones the source gives twice: independent, self-reliant, skeptical). Strength: plain in the source, plain in the draft.

label: gen-z
source_text: [Pew] anyone born from 1997 onward is part of a new generation The iPhone launched in 2007, when the oldest Gen Zers were 10. Social media, constant connectivity and on-demand entertainment and communication are innovations Millennials adapted to as they came of age. For those born after 1996, these are largely assumed. [...] [Wikipedia] with the generation typically being defined as people born from 1997 to 2012. Generation Z has been described as "better behaved and less hedonistic" than previous generations. They have fewer teenage pregnancies, consume less alcohol (but not necessarily less of other psychoactive drugs), and are more focused on school and job prospects. [...] There is greater awareness and diagnosis of mental health conditions among Generation Z, and sleep deprivation is more frequently reported.
description_draft: This means being born between 1997 and 2012: taking smartphones and social media for granted, better behaved, less hedonistic than earlier generations, focused on school and work, and open about mental health.
nearest_existing: young / plugged_in / well_behaved / risk_averse / health_conscious: young is age alone (teens or twenties); the typed version is the cohort (about 14 to 29 in 2026) with smartphones assumed, the better-behaved-less-hedonistic image, and openness about mental health; plugged_in is on the feeds all day at any age.
notes: Pew Research Center's 2019 definitions give the birth years and the formative events but no portrait; the conventional portrait is Wikipedia's, each sentence checked against the raw page. The queue's speech stereotypes (slang, typing habits) appear in none of the sources, so the draft carries habits and attitudes only; the label will have to carry the speech. Membership tag: the draft states the cohort plainly, no disclaimer. Pew gives only the start year (1997 onward); the 2012 end is Wikipedia's. 'Taking smartphones and social media for granted' renders Pew's 'For those born after 1996, these are largely assumed.' 'Open about mental health' renders Wikipedia's 'greater awareness and diagnosis of mental health conditions'. Strength: the source is mildly flattering (better behaved, less hedonistic, more focused on school) and the draft stays there; this member is the mildest of the four. Wikipedia's 'digital natives' nickname kept out.

label: influence (DISC)
source_text: The i (Influence) style is active and accepting. This describes people who are outgoing, enthusiastic, and lively. [...] People with DiSC styles at the top of the circle tend to be fast-paced and are often described as assertive, dynamic, and bold. [...] On the other hand, people with styles on the right side of the circle are naturally more receptive in nature and are often described as people-focused, empathizing, and agreeable.
description_draft: This means being fast-paced and accepting: outgoing, enthusiastic and lively, bold and dynamic in getting things moving, focused on people over logic, and agreeable toward others rather than skeptical of them.
nearest_existing: extroverted / gregarious / energetic / cheerful / charismatic: the typed version is the fast-paced-and-accepting quadrant, extroversion plus agreeableness; plain extroverted lacks the agreeable stance (and is about energy from company), cheerful lacks the pace.
notes: Primary source is the publisher's (Wiley, Everything DiSC) own page, since the four labels are the publisher's names; the fuller style pages with priorities and motivators (discprofile.com/what-is-disc and its overview-styles PDF) returned HTTP 403 to every fetch, so they are not quoted. A search-engine snippet of that page (unverified, not used in the draft) listed the D style's priorities as getting immediate results, taking action, challenging self and others; i as expressing enthusiasm, taking action, encouraging collaboration; S as giving support, maintaining stability, enjoying collaboration; C as ensuring accuracy, maintaining stability, challenging assumptions. Marston 1928, Emotions of Normal People (public domain; full text at https://archive.org/stream/emotionsofnormal0000mars/emotionsofnormal0000mars_djvu.txt), names the four primary emotions dominance, inducement, submission and compliance on two axes, alliance vs antagonism of the stimulus and superiority vs inferiority of the self's strength; dominance is "chiefly characterized by victory of the motor self over an antagonist of inferior intensity", inducement introspectively "a process of persuading someone, in a friendly way, to perform an act suggested by the subject", submission the bodily attitude of "an obedient child toward a loving mother", compliance that "the subject is moving himself at the dictates of a superior force". Wikipedia's gloss (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DISC_assessment): "Dominance: active use of force to overcome resistance in the environment Inducement: use of charm in order to deal with obstacles Submission: warm and voluntary acceptance of the need to fulfill a request Compliance: fearful adjustment to a superior force." The modern S and C differ from Marston's submission and compliance, so his text is background, not the summarised source. Strength: flattering in the source (outgoing, enthusiastic, lively), flattering in the draft.

label: killer (Bartle)
source_text: Killers get their kicks from imposing themselves on others. [...] Much more commonly, people attack other players with a view to killing off their personae (hence the name for this style of play). The more massive the distress caused, the greater the killer's joy at having caused it. Normal points-scoring is usually required so as to become powerful enough to begin causing havoc in earnest, and exploration of a kind is necessary to discover new and ingenious ways to kill people. [...] They're all just means to an end, though; only in the knowledge that a real person, somewhere, is very upset by what you've just done, yet can themselves do nothing about it, is there any true adrenalin-shooting, juicy fun.
description_draft: This means playing to impose oneself on other players: attacking and killing their characters, the greater the distress caused the better, and treating points, exploring and talk as mere means to that.
nearest_existing: bullying / cruel / ruthless_while_playing / competitive: ruthless_while_playing does for advantage in fiction what it would not do for real; the killer's object is not advantage but the other player's real distress. Bullying and cruel are the real-life cousins; the typed version is confined to play. Competitive wants to win; the killer wants the victim upset.
notes: Bartle 1996, 'Hearts, clubs, diamonds, spades: players who suit MUDs', Journal of MUD Research 1(1); the author's own page, fetched raw and quoted from it. Axes in Bartle's words: "The x-axis goes from an emphasis on players (left) to an emphasis on the environment (right); the y-axis goes from acting with (bottom) to acting on (top)." Bartle's quadrant glosses: "Achievers are interested in doing things to the game, ie. in ACTING on the WORLD." and "Explorers are interested in having the game surprise them, ie. in INTERACTING with the WORLD." The omitted sentence allows a 'nice' busybody variant that Bartle himself dismisses as rare. 'Characters' for Bartle's 'personae'. Strength: Bartle's paragraph is strong (joy at distress, a real person very upset and helpless) and the draft keeps it; the one Bartle member that is a vice.

label: millennial
source_text: [Pew] Anyone born between 1981 and 1996 (ages 23 to 38 in 2019) is considered a Millennial, and anyone born from 1997 onward is part of a new generation. [...] [Wikipedia] elevated familiarity with the Internet and technology in general, and usage of early social media platforms such as AOL Instant Messenger, LiveJournal, and Myspace. [...] Twenge attributes millennials with the traits of confidence and tolerance, but also describes a sense of entitlement and narcissism [...] with many facing high levels of youth unemployment, student debt, and childcare costs in the wake of the Great Recession [...] Across the globe, millennials and subsequent generations have postponed marriage or living together as a couple.
description_draft: This means being born between 1981 and 1996: growing up alongside the internet, entering work in a recession with student debt, confident and tolerant, early to social media and slow to marry.
nearest_existing: confident / plugged_in / financially_precarious / early_adopter: the typed version is the cohort (about 30 to 45 in 2026) shaped by the internet's arrival and the 2008 recession; plugged_in is on the feeds all day at any age, financially_precarious is a present condition not a cohort history.
notes: Pew Research Center's 2019 definitions give the birth years and the formative events but no portrait; the conventional portrait is Wikipedia's, each sentence checked against the raw page. The queue's speech stereotypes (slang, typing habits) appear in none of the sources, so the draft carries habits and attitudes only; the label will have to carry the speech. Membership tag: the draft states the cohort plainly, no disclaimer. Pew also records 9/11 (most were 5 to 20) and the Iraq and Afghanistan wars as formative; the draft keeps the recession (Pew: 'the height of an economic recession', a 'slow start') through Wikipedia's student-debt sentence and leaves 9/11 out at 32 words. Wikipedia's lead gives Pew's years. FLAG for Roger: the 'entitlement and narcissism' stereotype is in the source as Twenge's claim, immediately followed by a critic ('vastly misinterpreting or over-interpreting the data'), so it is contested there; the draft keeps her uncontested pair, confident and tolerant, and leaves entitled out. If the trait is meant to carry the popular stereotype, 'entitled' belongs in, at the cost of a word. 'Echo Boomers' and 'digital natives' nicknames kept out. Strength: plain in the source, plain in the draft.

label: neglectful (Baumrind)
source_text: Uninvolved parents are low in both responsiveness and demandingness. In extreme cases, this parenting style might encompass both rejecting-neglecting and neglectful parents, although most parents of this type fall within the normal range. [...] Parental responsiveness (also referred to as parental warmth or supportiveness) refers to "the extent to which parents intentionally foster individuality, self-regulation, and self-assertion by being attuned, supportive, and acquiescent to children's special needs and demands" (Baumrind, 1991, p. 62). Parental demandingness (also referred to as behavioral control) refers to "the claims parents make on children to become integrated into the family whole, by their maturity demands, supervision, disciplinary efforts and willingness to confront the child who disobeys" (Baumrind, 1991, pp. 61-62). [...] [Wikipedia, Parenting styles] They may provide basic necessities such as food, shelter, and clothing, but they do not indulge their children's emotions or opinions.
description_draft: This means being neither warm nor demanding with one's children: rarely supervising, disciplining or asking maturity of them and, beyond food and shelter, paying little attention to what they feel or do.
nearest_existing: neglectful (plain: leaving those in one's care to fend for themselves, no notice of harm) / hands_off / absentee / uncaring: the typed version is the parent low on both warmth and demands, within the normal range per the source, so markedly milder than plain neglectful; plain neglectful is the nurturing pair's vice, this is a quadrant.
notes: Maccoby & Martin 1983 (Handbook of Child Psychology vol. 4) is not open online; quoted as presented in Nancy Darling, 'Parenting Style and Its Correlates', ERIC Digest ED427896 (1999), which attributes the four-fold typology and the uninvolved corner to them ("Categorizing parents according to whether they are high or low on parental demandingness and responsiveness creates a typology of four parenting styles: indulgent, authoritarian, authoritative, and uninvolved (Maccoby & Martin, 1983).") and gives Baumrind 1991's definitions of the two dimensions. The PDF's text layer had no spaces; spaces were restored by hand and the quotes checked against the extracted text with spaces removed. Secondary (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parenting_styles): 'The parent is not responsive and not demanding.' and 'Neglectful parenting, also known as uninvolved, detached, dismissive, or hands-off parenting, is characterized by a lack of warmth and control. Neglectful parents are unaware of what their children are doing, and if they find out, they feel indifferent towards them. They may provide basic necessities such as food, shelter, and clothing, but they do not indulge their children's emotions or opinions.' The draft's 'beyond food and shelter' comes from this. FLAG for Roger: the scholarly source is a placement (low on both) with a hedge ('most parents of this type fall within the normal range'), so the draft is mild, as the strength rule requires; Wikipedia's version is stronger (unaware, indifferent). The draft's 'rarely supervising, disciplining or asking maturity of them' is Baumrind 1991's demandingness list (maturity demands, supervision, disciplinary efforts) negated. The queue's label 'neglectful' is Maccoby & Martin's; Darling's is 'uninvolved'.

label: permissive (Baumrind)
source_text: The permissive parent attempts to behave in a nonpunitive, acceptant and affirmative manner towards the child's impulses, desires, and actions. She [parent] consults with him [child] about policy decisions and gives explanations for family rules. She makes few demands for household responsibility and orderly behavior. She presents herself to the child as a resource for him to use as he wishes, not as an ideal for him to emulate, nor as an active agent responsible for shaping or altering his ongoing or future behavior. She allows the child to regulate his own activities as much as possible, avoids the exercise of control, and does not encourage him to obey externally defined standards. She attempts to use reason and manipulation, but not overt power to accomplish her ends
description_draft: This means accepting one's children's impulses rather than punishing them: asking little in chores or tidiness, letting them regulate themselves, and being a resource to draw on, not an authority to obey.
nearest_existing: permissive (plain: letting sex, drink, drugs and foul language pass) / lenient / hands_off: the typed version is the parent accepting a child's impulses and making few demands; plain permissive is tolerance of vice, lenient is keeping the bar low for people generally, hands_off is walking away from delegated work.
notes: Baumrind 1966, p. 889, as quoted on the same teaching page. 'A resource to draw on, not an authority to obey' renders 'presents herself to the child as a resource for him to use as he wishes, not as an ideal for him to emulate' and 'does not encourage him to obey externally defined standards'; 'chores or tidiness' renders 'household responsibility and orderly behavior'. Left out at 32 words: 'consults with him about policy decisions' and 'uses reason and manipulation, but not overt power'. Strength: Baumrind's permissive is written neutrally (acceptant, affirmative, few demands) and the draft matches; it is milder than the corpus's lenient.

label: socializer (Bartle)
source_text: Socialisers are interested in people, and what they have to say. The game is merely a backdrop, a common ground where things happen to players. Inter-player relationships are important: empathising with people, sympathising, joking, entertaining, listening; even merely observing people play can be rewarding - seeing them grow as individuals, maturing over time. Some exploration may be necessary so as to understand what everyone else is talking about, and points-scoring could be required to gain access to neat communicative spells available only to higher levels (as well as to obtain a certain status in the community). Killing, however, is something only ever to be excused if it's a futile, impulsive act of revenge, perpetrated upon someone who has caused intolerable pain to a dear friend. The only ultimately fulfilling thing is not how to rise levels or kill hapless drips; it's getting to know people, to undertand them, and to form beautiful, lasting relationships.
description_draft: This means playing for the people: the game is a backdrop for meeting, listening, joking, sympathizing and forming lasting friendships; levels and maps matter only as aids to conversation, killing almost never.
nearest_existing: gregarious / friendly / other_focused: the plain traits are sociability in general; the typed version is sociability as the reason to play, with the game a venue for talk and lasting friendships, and the other three ways of playing valued only as far as they serve that.
notes: Bartle 1996, 'Hearts, clubs, diamonds, spades: players who suit MUDs', Journal of MUD Research 1(1); the author's own page, fetched raw and quoted from it. Axes in Bartle's words: "The x-axis goes from an emphasis on players (left) to an emphasis on the environment (right); the y-axis goes from acting with (bottom) to acting on (top)." Bartle's quadrant glosses: "Achievers are interested in doing things to the game, ie. in ACTING on the WORLD." and "Explorers are interested in having the game surprise them, ie. in INTERACTING with the WORLD." Bartle's 'undertand' is his typo, reproduced. 'Killing almost never' renders Bartle's 'only ever to be excused if it's a futile, impulsive act of revenge' for a friend. US 'socializer' / 'sympathizing' against Bartle's British spellings. Strength: warm in the source ('beautiful, lasting relationships'), warm in the draft.

label: steadiness (DISC)
source_text: The S (Steadiness) style is thoughtful and accepting. This describes people who are gentle, accommodating, and patient with others’ mistakes. [...] Conversely, people with styles that fall toward the bottom of the circle tend to be more moderate-paced and are often described as calm, methodical, and careful. [...] On the other hand, people with styles on the right side of the circle are naturally more receptive in nature and are often described as people-focused, empathizing, and agreeable.
description_draft: This means being moderate-paced and accepting: gentle, accommodating and patient with others' mistakes, calm and careful in how one works, focused on people over logic, and empathizing and agreeable rather than challenging.
nearest_existing: steady (plain: holding the same tone and view through a conversation) / accommodating / patient / gentle: plain steady is consistency of position, not this; the typed version is the calm, accepting, people-focused style, accommodating plus patient plus a moderate pace, so the shared word is misleading (Marston's original factor was submission).
notes: Primary source is the publisher's (Wiley, Everything DiSC) own page, since the four labels are the publisher's names; the fuller style pages with priorities and motivators (discprofile.com/what-is-disc and its overview-styles PDF) returned HTTP 403 to every fetch, so they are not quoted. A search-engine snippet of that page (unverified, not used in the draft) listed the D style's priorities as getting immediate results, taking action, challenging self and others; i as expressing enthusiasm, taking action, encouraging collaboration; S as giving support, maintaining stability, enjoying collaboration; C as ensuring accuracy, maintaining stability, challenging assumptions. Marston 1928, Emotions of Normal People (public domain; full text at https://archive.org/stream/emotionsofnormal0000mars/emotionsofnormal0000mars_djvu.txt), names the four primary emotions dominance, inducement, submission and compliance on two axes, alliance vs antagonism of the stimulus and superiority vs inferiority of the self's strength; dominance is "chiefly characterized by victory of the motor self over an antagonist of inferior intensity", inducement introspectively "a process of persuading someone, in a friendly way, to perform an act suggested by the subject", submission the bodily attitude of "an obedient child toward a loving mother", compliance that "the subject is moving himself at the dictates of a superior force". Wikipedia's gloss (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DISC_assessment): "Dominance: active use of force to overcome resistance in the environment Inducement: use of charm in order to deal with obstacles Submission: warm and voluntary acceptance of the need to fulfill a request Compliance: fearful adjustment to a superior force." The modern S and C differ from Marston's submission and compliance, so his text is background, not the summarised source. Strength: flattering in the source (gentle, accommodating, patient), flattering in the draft; markedly milder than any corpus vice and near the corpus's agreeable cluster.
